messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jose Rodríguez, a 62‑year‑old dancer from a modest family in East Los Angeles, remembers the day his world shattered with a raw, unfiltered clarity. He was driving home from a late‑night rehearsal, the stage lights still flashing faintly in his memory, when a freight truck, swerving on the interstate, collided with his sedan. The impact was sudden and violent; the airbags deployed, the dashboard shattered, and Jose felt his body jerked forward as if it had been pulled apart and thrown against the glass. He was ejected from the vehicle, blood seeping into his mouth, and an ambulance rushed him to the hospital with a lingering metallic taste in his lungs. The terror of that instant still lingers, and the images that haunt him are not the polished choreography of his life but the screech of tires, the flash of headlights, and a sudden, overwhelming sense of doom. Because Jose swore that he would never feel normal emotions again, that life could never be the same, and that the accident must have been his fault, he began to view each new space as a potential threat. The helplessness he felt—his sense that bad things would inevitably happen—made him scan every room for an exit as soon as he entered. In the studio where he rehearsed, he would pause, eyes darting from the doorway to the mirrors, looking for a way out if the floor suddenly gave way. The startle he felt at a casual touch—an assistant’s hand brushing his arm to adjust his shoes—seemed a harbinger of a possible repeat of that collision. He had come to believe that every sudden movement could trigger a return to that life‑threatening moment. Those constant, anxious scans fed back into his memories of the crash. When the lights dimmed in a rehearsal hall, the echo of the screeching tires would flicker in his mind, and he would hear the frantic shouts he had overheard that day—voices like the crash’s own soundtrack. The images were hard to put into words; his mind struggled to translate the terrifying scene into a coherent narrative, and the memories stayed locked in the nonverbal, sensory realm. The shame that surged whenever he recalled the event intensified the intrusion, making each recall a painful echo of his earlier trauma. The fragmentation of his memory pushed Jose toward deliberate avoidance tactics. He would consciously dissociate, feeling his body separate from the scene as if he were watching it from a distance. He stayed awake long into the night, delaying sleep until the early hours, hoping to outrun the lingering nightmares. He would suppress thoughts about the accident, forcing himself to ignore the image of his own crumpled car whenever it surfaced. These strategies were his way of protecting himself from the intense shame and terror that came with the memories. Yet each time Jose suppressed the trauma, the memory’s emotional content sharpened. The more he denied the details, the louder the auditory echoes of the truck’s engine and the collision’s roar seemed to his ears. His deliberate dissociation left the vivid sensory traces unprocessed, reinforcing the memory’s vivid, nonverbal nature. He found himself hearing the same sounds of crunching metal and hearing the same shouts whenever he stepped into a crowded room, and his attempts to ignore these memories only made them more intrusive. Jose’s coping tactics further hardened his negative beliefs about himself. He began to see that his emotional numbness was a permanent condition, that his sense of helplessness was not just a fleeting feeling but a permanent trait, and that the accident had revealed his inherent flaw—a character he blamed himself for. These convictions, in turn, amplified his threat perception: every sudden movement, every unfamiliar face, became a reminder of his perceived inadequacy and vulnerability. He stopped attending group rehearsals because the thought of another person touching him in a crowd set his heart racing. He avoided even the simple act of stepping onto the studio floor, for fear it might spark a return to that car wreck. The cumulative weight of these loops—hypervigilance, intrusive memory, maladaptive avoidance, and entrenched negative beliefs—had taken a toll on Jose’s life. He missed weeks of choreography, and his wife, María, noticed his growing withdrawal and the way his eyes would dart nervously whenever a light flickered on. When he finally reached out to a therapist, it was after a rehearsal in which a colleague's accidental brush of his shoulder set off a full‑blown panic attack that left him physically shaking and unable to finish a routine. He feared that if he did not seek help, the memory would consume every moment of his dancing and his marriage, and he yearned for relief from the constant fear that the next collision might come in a sudden, silent, unavoidable form.
